source_text: Sed proh Dei nostri atque hominum fidem! Haeccine potuisse commentorum prodigia reperiri, ut dedita opera impensoque studio in perversum conentur omnia asserere! Quid enim tam prodigiale, quam quod Poenus eloquitur? Ea, inquit, quae erant naturalia, perpetua non fuerunt; et illa, quae studio suscepta sunt, primis coagulis adhaesere membrorum. Bonus, inquit, Adam factus est, habuit innocentiam naturalem; ceteris etiam creaturis peculiari nobilitate praelatus, similitudine sui Conditoris enituit. Liberum arbitrium in conditione suscepit, ut in quam vellet partem suopte iudicio moveretur, facultatemque vel ad bonum, vel ad malum accedendi, vel ab utroque recedendi, ipsa facturae suae, qua ceteris antistabat, conditione sortitus est. Sed quoniam emancipato iudicio usurpavit pravam animi liberi voluntatem, illa omnia, quae ingenita constabat, evertit; solumque peccatum et peccandi necessitas ei inseparabiliter adhaesit. Hoc est, quod dixi prodigiale commentum. Inaudita quippe deformitas est dicere: Bene institutum est animal, in quo amissibilia fuerunt bona etiam naturalia, cui inseparabiliter adhaeserunt mala vel voluntaria.
pass_a_gloss: But oh the faith of our God and of humans! Could these portents of inventions have been found, that with dedicated work and expended study they try to assert all things into the perverse! For what so portentous, as what the Punic utters? Those things, he says, which were natural were not perpetual; and those which were taken up by study stuck to the first coagulations of the members. Adam, he says, was made good, he had a natural innocence; preferred even to the rest of creatures by a peculiar nobility, he shone by a likeness of his Founder. He received free decision in the condition, that he would be moved by his own judgment toward which part he willed, and a faculty either of approaching good or evil, or of receding from each, he received by the very condition of his making, by which he stood before the rest. But because by an emancipated judgment he usurped a crooked will of a free mind, he overturned all those things which stood as inborn; and only sin and a necessity of sinning stuck to him inseparably. This is what I called a portentous invention. For it is an unheard deformity to say: The animal was well instituted, in which even natural goods were losable, to which evils even voluntary stuck inseparably.

lemmas.lexica: LS naturalis; Blaise malum naturale=evil as a nature
LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will
LS arbitrium=judgment, free decision; Blaise liberum arbitrium
LS liber=free; Blaise unde liberum est abstinere
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself

pass_b_english: But by the faithfulness of our God and of humanity! Could such monstrous inventions really have been devised, deliberately and laboriously trying to assert everything upside down? What could be more monstrous than what the Carthaginian says? Things that were natural, he says, did not endure; things adopted by choice adhered to the first formation of the bodily members.

Adam, he says, was made good and possessed natural innocence. Raised above other creatures by a special nobility, he shone with his Creator’s likeness (Genesis 1:26–27). He received free will in his created condition, to move by his own judgment in whatever direction he wished. Through the very condition of his making, which set him above the rest, he obtained the ability to approach either good or evil and withdraw from either. But because he used his independent judgment to adopt a corrupt inclination of the free mind, he overthrew all those admittedly inborn things; only sin and the necessity of sinning clung to him inseparably.
This is what I called a monstrous invention. It is an unheard-of disgrace to say: A living being was well made in whom even natural goods could be lost, while even voluntary evils clung inseparably.

choices.why: Glossary default: arbitrium is the decision-power, not a later Augustinian/Reformation free-will locus.
Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
Freedom to abstain is required for will and sin.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

bible_refs.note: From Pass B Scripture tagging; wording follows Julian's Latin, not a modern Bible.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
